nameStory: Little-robin gets its charming name from its small, delicate appearance and reddish-tinged stems and leaves that reminded early botanists of a robin's breast. The "little" part distinguishes it from its close cousin Herb Robert, which is also sometimes called "robin" but grows larger and more robust.
description: Little-robin is a small, delicate annual wildflower that rarely grows taller than 8 inches. This tiny member of the geranium family has deeply divided, lacy leaves and produces small pink or purple flowers throughout the growing season. The entire plant often takes on reddish hues, especially the stems and leaf edges, giving it a distinctive appearance among New England's smaller wildflowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink to purple flowers, usually less than half an inch across, with five rounded petals that have a papery, delicate texture when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, lacy leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, often with reddish edges that become more pronounced in cool weather

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Very small, low-growing annual that forms compact mounds rarely exceeding 8 inches tall, with a sprawling habit

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops the characteristic "crane's bill" seed pods that split explosively when ripe, launching seeds several feet away with an audible pop

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, often reddish stems that feel slightly hairy and become more intensely colored in direct sunlight or cool temperatures

habitat: Little-robin is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region. When found, it typically grows in disturbed soils, along roadsides, or in waste places where other vegetation is sparse. It prefers well-drained, sandy or rocky soils in sunny to partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic lacy, reddish-tinged leaves becoming visible in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Blooming period with small pink to purple flowers appearing continuously, while the reddish coloration in stems and leaf edges intensifies in the heat.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to set their explosive seed pods and the entire plant takes on deeper red hues before dying back with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, little-robin dies completely and exists only as seeds waiting in the soil for the next growing season.

funFact: Like other crane's-bill geraniums, little-robin has explosive seed pods that can launch their seeds up to 15 feet away with enough force to make an audible popping sound - it's nature's own tiny catapult system!
confusionNotes: Little-robin looks very similar to its larger cousin Herb Robert, but little-robin stays much smaller (under 8 inches vs. Herb Robert's 12+ inches) and has a more compact, mounded growth habit rather than Herb Robert's more upright, spreading form. Memory trick: "Little-robin stays little."
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these wild geraniums with the colorful potted geraniums sold at garden centers - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like little-robin are sometimes called "hardy geraniums" and are completely different plants, though they're in the same family.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert. While wild geranium has larger, showier pink flowers and grows in woodlands, little-robin prefers disturbed ground and has much smaller, more delicate blooms. Its compact size and intensely reddish coloration make it unique among the region's geraniums.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
